1 Introduction
Casino games are designed to make gamblers choose from a range of negative expected value outcomes.
In the short run, a gambler may proﬁt; however, in the long run, th e house always wins due to the Law
of Large Numbers. The sentiment of the house inevitably winning is pa ralleled in ﬁnancial markets by the
strong form of the Eﬃcient Markets Hypothesis (Fama 1970), whic h states that it is impossible to outperform
the market due to the informational eﬃciency of markets.
While there are some similarities in market structure between ﬁnancia l markets and casino sports
books, there are also several key diﬀerences (Levitt 2004). In ﬁ nancial markets, price is dictated by supply
and demand. However, in sports betting markets, each casino dict ates the “price” (odds ratio) at which
the “stock” (speciﬁc bet) will trade. Levitt stresses the importa nce of the casino providing the right price
for each bet by mentioning that the bookmaker can be exposed to s igniﬁcant losses if the price set by the
bookmaker is incorrect. Another key diﬀerence between ﬁnancial markets and sports betting markets is that
the Securities and Exchange Commission requires brokers to execu te trades at the National Best Bid and
Oﬀer, whereas it is up to the individual bettor to discover which casin o is oﬀering the best risk-reward ratio.
As Moskowitz (2015) notes, several papers 1 study the eﬃciency of sports betting markets, with the
evidence somewhat mixed. We deﬁne an ineﬃcient sports betting mar ket as a market in which a betting
strategy consistently generates proﬁt. (Snyder 1978; Sauer e t al 1988; Constantinou et al 2013). From our
analysis, we ﬁnd that there are exploitable ineﬃciencies due to diﬀere nces in price oﬀerings by individual
casinos. Unlike any of the aforementioned papers (which tend to fo cus on one or two sports), we utilize
a single pricing model to identify mispriced bets across several spor ts (namely the NFL, NBA, NCAAF,
NCAAB, and WNBA). We extend Levitt’s conclusion that bookmakers are more skilled at predicting game
outcomes than bettors to the other major sports that we examin e in this paper. This assumption that
bookmakers are the most skilled at predicting game outcomes is key t o formulating our model as we chieﬂy
use information and data gathered from the entire market of casin os to take advantage of the mispricing by
ineﬃcient casinos. Due to our successful identiﬁcations of mispricin gs in sports betting markets, we were
able to build a betting strategy that consistently generates proﬁt across several diﬀerent sports.
1 Snyder (1978), Vergin and Scriabin (1978), Ali (1979), Lose y and Talbott (1980), Hausch et al (1981), Asch et al (1984),
Zuber et al (1985), Thaler and Ziemba (1988), Sauer et al (198 8), Gandar et al (1988), Camerer (1989), Golec and Tamarkin
(1991), W oodland and W oodland (1994), Dare and MacDonald (1 996), Gray and Gray (1997), Avery and Chevalier (1999),
Kuypers (2000), and Lee and Smith (2002) have commented on th e eﬃciency of various sports betting markets.
1

2 Terminology
Before diving deeper into the subject matter, we ﬁnd it essential t o deﬁne some of the parlance involved
with sports betting.
2.1 Point Spread & Spread Bets
To paraphrase Stern (1991), the perceived diﬀerence between t wo sporting teams is measured by the
point spread. For example, if Team A is determined to have a point spr ead of -6.5 when matched up against
Team B, then Team A is favored to beat Team B by 6.5 points. In this sc enario, Team A is the favorite (as
they are favored to win) and Team B is the underdog. A bet placed on Team A will be a winning bet if
and only if Team A beats Team B by more than 6.5 points. Conversely, T eam B will have an inverse point
spread of +6.5 points. A bet placed on Team B will be a winning bet if and o nly if Team B either wins or
loses by less than 6.5 points. The betting in this scenario is an example o f a spread bet. A spread bet is
designed to have even odds, meaning that chance of success and f ailure are equal at 50%. For this reason, a
spread bet generally pays out 91 cents for every dollar wagered if t he bet is successful. The casino collects
the other 9 cents, which is called a “vigorish”. If there is an equal am ount of money on either side, then the
casino collects 9 cents for each dollar risked, and is exposed to no ris k.
Spreads can also be understood in the following manner, where P F S represents the Projected Final
Score of each team.
Point Spread = P F SF avorite− P F SU nderdog (1)
Spreads often include the half point “hook” in order to avoid ties, as most major sports (basketball,
football, soccer, hockey, etc.) do not have fractional point scor es. In the event that the spread is a whole
number (i.e. Team A is +6), and the outcome is Team A wins by 6 points, m oney is returned to anyone
who bets on the game. This kind of event is called a “push”.
2.2 Moneyline Bets
The Moneyline bet is a wager on which team will win. Moskowitz mentions t hat Moneyline bets pay
out various amounts of dollars depending on which team is bet. (Mosk owitz 2015). For example, if the
moneyline for Team A is -500 and the moneyline for Team B is +300, a suc cessful wager of 500 dollars on
Team A nets a 100 dollar proﬁt while a successful wager of 100 dollars on Team B nets a 300 dollar proﬁt.
Our algorithm solely focuses on identifying mispriced moneyline bets.
2

2.3 Market Return
Deﬁning average market return in the sports betting context is imp ortant since this activity does not
lend itself to traditional ﬁnancial return concepts, such as a comp arison to given benchmarks. A bettor’s
average return in this market will be equal to the mean return of th eir wagers, weighted for bet sizes. Table
1 reveals that a bettor who randomly wagers on spread bets will hav e a mean return of approximately -4.4%
for all sports, and a bettor who randomly wagers on moneyline bets will have a mean return between -6.4%

3 Model & Data
3.1 Probability and Expected Value
There are 16 casino sportsbooks in Las Vegas that we obtained dat a from. For any given sports game,
at most 16 casinos will provide point spreads and moneyline betting od ds. The point spread and moneyline
odds vary from casino to casino. Thus, from our obtained data, we end up with a range of point spreads and
moneyline odds. As there are are a plethora of teams in College Baske tball and College Football, we only
considered games where one team was a member of a “Power Five” co nference2. For all other sports, we
considered all games between all teams, excluding pre-season (ex hibition) games but including post-season
(i.e. playoﬀ) games.
Our algorithm utilizes this range of point spreads to determine the pr obability of a team winning the
game. Unlike Stern, we do not assume that a team’s implied probability o f winning a game from the point
spread is normally distributed. One limitation of Stern’s model is its abilit y to only price games with the
absolute value of the spread less than six. Our model is non-parame tric and allows us to price moneyline
bets for any point spread. The following equation describes our Bay esian formula for a team’s likelihood to
win a game, at point spread PS.
P(Win| PS) = Historical Win % of T eams with Point Spread = PS (2)
This formula is the engine of our algorithm. We theorize that a team at point spread PS will win at
2 The Power Five Conferences are deﬁned to be the Atlantic Coas t Conference, Big Ten Conference, Big 12 Conference,
Pac-12 Conference, and Southeastern Conference.
3

the same rate at which historical teams at spread PS have won. Res ults that are considered in determining
the rate at which historical teams win only include games that have co ncluded before the game that we wish
to price. If we know the probability of an event, and we know the pay out for making a correct wager, we
can deﬁne expected value for a one dollar bet as follows.
Expected V alue = [P(Winning)∗ Payout]− P(Losing) (3)
The expected value of a one dollar bet is deﬁned as the probability of w inning multiplied by the payout
for winning, subtracted by the probability of losing multiplied by the mo ney wagered. Since the money
wagered in a one dollar bet is 1, the expected winnings are now solely su btracted by the probability of
losing. This is how Equation 3 is formed. The expected value of a bet sy mbolizes the expected money made
or lost from the bet. Theoretically, selecting bets that have a posit ive expected value, and betting on them,
would generate proﬁt over time. This is the foundation of our bettin g algorithm.
Clearly, calculating the probability and expected value requires the s preads and payouts from Vegas
casinos and historical spread data and results (i.e. which teams won and lost). Vegasinsider.com has spread
and payout data from Vegas casinos for many sporting events, as well as the results of these events. In order
to properly price a game, we need the historical win percentage for teams at various spreads. From a variety
of sites, we obtained historical spread data and results ranging fr om 1990 to 2017.
3.2 Algorithms
As mentioned earlier, a range of point spreads and moneylines are ob tained from vegasinsider.com. As
we assume that the bookmakers know how to predict game outcome s best and are incentivized to provide
accurate prices (resulting in the market as a whole being information ally eﬃcient), we prefer to obtain the
most updated spreads and moneylines. Our data analysis agreed wit h this assumption, and revealed that
bookmakers’ last update (i.e. whether a player was injured, etc.) g enerally occurred within an hour of the
game. From this ﬁnding, we decided that the casino’s last update was the most accurate indicator of the
various casino speciﬁed variables (point spread and moneyline payou t), as it was closest to game time and
thus contained the most recent information.
We have two slightly diﬀerent strategies that utilize the range of spr eads to ﬁnd the probability of
winning, which we will refer to as “Simple” (Algorithm 1) and “Weighted” (Algorithm 2). Both algorithms
utilize an input mapping of spreads to their respective probabilities, b ut the Weighted algorithm also uses
an input mapping of spreads to their respective frequencies. The s imple algorithm returns the probability of
a team winning via calculating the simple average of the probabilities of t he unique spreads. The weighted

3.3 Epsilon and Expected Value Thresholds
As the returns in Table 2 will demonstrate, simply betting on all games with positive expected value
generates positive return on investment for three out of ﬁve spo rts when the simple algorithm is used to
calculate probability of winning, and ﬁve out of ﬁve sports when the w eighted algorithm is used to calculate
the probability of winning. This ﬁnding implies that there are ineﬃciencie s in the market, as there exists
a method of obtaining positive returns. For reference, randomize d betting returns on the same data are
provided in Table 1. Both of these tables will be analyzed in further de tail in the Results section of the
paper. From data analysis, we were able to make improvements on ou r model.
The ﬁrst improvement on our model regards the issue of predicting games with large spreads. This
scenario is why Stern’s model works best pricing bets with the absolu te value of the spread less than six, as
the tails are hard to predict. If the spread is large, it implies that one team is heavily favored to beat the other
team, and our model lacks the historical sample size at such large sp reads to create a realistic probability
estimate. Additionally, casinos make the payouts for betting on und erdogs in this scenario ludicrously high,
resulting in the model generating a high expected value for underdo gs in these cases.
To account for the eﬀect of these games in the tails, we created th e “Epsilon Threshold”. The goal
of the Epsilon Threshold is to provide a symmetric set of bounds for t he probabilities of teams winning
games that we are willing to bet on when the bet has positive expected value. For bets outside the bounds,
we always go with the probability favorite. After determining which Ep silon Value yields the highest total
return on investment, we can deﬁne the optimal bettable range of winning percentages as: ( . 5− ǫ, . 5 + ǫ).
The optimal Epsilon value varies signiﬁcantly from sport to sport.
5

The second improvement we designed is the “Expected Value Thresh old”. Expected Value Threshold
is the the value of Expected Value that a bet must be greater than in order to place the bet. The default
Expected Value Threshold that we use is 0. In this default case, any bet that has a positive Expected Value
will be bet on. In general, as the Expected Value Threshold increase s so does the return on investment,
which leads us to believe that the model is detecting large ineﬃciencies very well.

of the bet and applying the epsilon and expected value thresholds. T he algorithm takes the following inputs:
the expected value of betting on the favorite, the expected value of betting on the underdog, the probability
that the favorite wins, the probability that the underdog wins, the value of the epsilon hyper-parameter,
and the value of the expected value threshold. The output of the a lgorithm is a decision to bet on the
favorite, underdog, or neither team depending on the ﬁltering crit eria of expected value, epsilon threshold,

5 Conclusion
Levitt (2004) succinctly states that there is little evidence of bett ors who are able to beat the bookies
systematically. For horseracing bets, Asch et al (1982) were not able to devise a successful strategy based
solely on observable betting odds. Through our analysis, we have sh own that we have created a betting
algorithm that solely relies upon betting odds and is capable of genera ting proﬁt for multiple sports con-
currently. If the market is eﬃcient, there should not be any skillful way to generate above average market
returns in the long run. Through our research and successful alg orithm, we demonstrated the existence
of market ineﬃciencies in sports betting markets. Our paper is the ﬁ rst to propose a single theory which
identiﬁes ineﬃciencies across sports through generating positive r eturns.
We encourage future researchers to further explore the beneﬁ ts and costs of using compounding bets
rather than independent $1 bets that we used in this paper, as well as properly utilizing Kelly’s portfolio
growth criterion (Kelly 1956). In addition, we also leave it to future r esearchers to propose improvements
on our win probability models and betting algorithm parameters.

    from __future__ import annotations

    import pandas as pd

    from quant_fund_agent.factors.base import BaseFactor
    from quant_fund_agent.factors.ops import rank, returns
    from quant_fund_agent.factors.registry import register_factor


    def _variance_ratio(ret: pd.DataFrame, k: int, n: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Lo–MacKinlay variance ratio over horizon k, estimated on a trailing
        n-bar window.  VR < 1 => mean-reverting, VR > 1 => trending.  Causal:
        every term is a trailing rolling statistic, so value at t sees only <= t."""
        var_1 = ret.rolling(n, min_periods=n).var()
        k_ret = ret.rolling(k, min_periods=k).sum()          # overlapping k-bar returns
        var_k = k_ret.rolling(n, min_periods=n).var()
        return var_k / (k * var_1).replace(0.0, np.nan)


    @register_factor
    class VarianceRatioReversion(BaseFactor):
        factor_id = "variance_ratio_reversion"
        name = "Variance-ratio reversion"
        category = "mean_reversion"
        description = (
            "Cross-sectional rank of (1 - trailing variance ratio): long the "
            "most mean-reverting names, short the most trending ones."
        )
        window_length = 120
        inputs = ["close"]
        prediction_horizon = 12
        suggested_horizons = [6, 12, 24]

        def calc(self, data: dict[str, pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame:
            ret = returns(data)
            vr = _variance_ratio(ret, 5, 100)
            return rank(1.0 - vr)

from __future__ import annotations

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from quant_fund_agent.factors.base import BaseFactor
from quant_fund_agent.factors.ops import (
    covariance,
    decay_linear,
    indneutralize,
    rank,
    stddev,
    ts_mean,
)
from quant_fund_agent.factors.registry import register_factor


def _volume_surprise(volume: pd.DataFrame, n: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Trailing standardized bar-volume surprise (causal z-score of log1p volume)."""
    lv = np.log1p(volume.fillna(0.0).clip(lower=0.0))
    mu = ts_mean(lv, n)
    sd = stddev(lv, n).replace(0.0, np.nan)
    z = (lv - mu) / sd
    return z.clip(-5.0, 5.0)


def _broadcast_row(series: pd.Series, template: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Broadcast a per-bar scalar series across every column of ``template``."""
    vals = np.repeat(series.to_numpy(dtype=float).reshape(-1, 1), template.shape[1], axis=1)
    return pd.DataFrame(vals, index=template.index, columns=template.columns)


def _rolling_loading(y: pd.DataFrame, x: pd.DataFrame, n: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Trailing OLS loading of y on x (cov/var over the last n bars, no intercept bias).

    Purely trailing: every element at t uses only bars <= t.
    """
    var_x = (stddev(x, n) ** 2).replace(0.0, np.nan)
    beta = covariance(y, x, n) / var_x
    return beta.clip(0.0, 3.0)


def _vol_scaled_logret(close: pd.DataFrame, n: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Log return divided by its own trailing volatility, so names are comparable."""
    px = close.replace(0.0, np.nan)
    lr = np.log(px) - np.log(px.shift(1))
    sd = stddev(lr, n).replace(0.0, np.nan)
    return (lr / sd).clip(-6.0, 6.0)


def _flow_path_integral(flow: pd.DataFrame, ret: pd.DataFrame, k: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Linear-decay-weighted trailing path integral of returns earned per unit of flow.

    This is the discrete two-channel path integral  sum_j w_j * flow_{t-j} * r_{t-j}
    with newest bars weighted most heavily - i.e. the return manufactured on that
    particular flow channel over the recent path.
    """
    prod = (flow * ret).replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan).fillna(0.0)
    return decay_linear(prod, k)


def _eligibility(data: dict, template: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Point-in-time 'acceptance eligibility' score in [0, 1] (higher = more eligible).

    Built from cross-sectional ranks of interest coverage, current ratio, (minus)
    debt-to-assets and market cap.  Fundamentals are quarterly step functions, so
    every leg is defensively filled to the neutral 0.5 when missing.
    """
    parts = []

    ic = data.get("interestCoverage")
    if isinstance(ic, pd.DataFrame):
        parts.append(rank(ic.reindex_like(template)).fillna(0.5))

    cr = data.get("currentRatio")
    if isinstance(cr, pd.DataFrame):
        parts.append(rank(cr.reindex_like(template)).fillna(0.5))

    dta = data.get("debtToAssets")
    if isinstance(dta, pd.DataFrame):
        parts.append(1.0 - rank(dta.reindex_like(template)).fillna(0.5))

    mc = data.get("marketCap")
    if isinstance(mc, pd.DataFrame):
        parts.append(rank(mc.reindex_like(template)).fillna(0.5))

    if not parts:
        return pd.DataFrame(0.5, index=template.index, columns=template.columns)

    acc = parts[0] * 0.0
    for p in parts:
        acc = acc + p
    elig = acc / float(len(parts))
    return elig.clip(0.0, 1.0).fillna(0.5)


@register_factor
class AcceptanceEligibilityGatedNegotiableFlowSplit(BaseFactor):
    """Fade returns earned on common ('negotiable') volume, ride returns earned on
    residual specialist volume, with both legs tilted by balance-sheet eligibility."""

    factor_id = "acceptance_eligibility_gated_negotiable_flow_split"
    name = "Negotiable vs Idiosyncratic Flow Split, Gated by Credit-Standing Eligibility"
    category = "microstructure"
    description = (
        "Splits each name's standardized bar-volume surprise into a common part "
        "(causal rolling loading on the cross-sectional median surprise) and an "
        "idiosyncratic residual, forms decay-weighted path integrals of vol-scaled "
        "log returns earned on each flow channel, and outputs the sector-neutralized "
        "combination -w_common*R_common + w_idio*R_idio with weights tilted by a "
        "point-in-time acceptance-eligibility score (interestCoverage, currentRatio, "
        "debtToAssets, marketCap ranks)."
    )
    window_length = 200
    inputs = [
        "close",
        "volume",
        "sector",
        "interestCoverage",
        "currentRatio",
        "debtToAssets",
        "marketCap",
    ]
    prediction_horizon = 6
    suggested_horizons = [6]

    # --- windows (bars of 10 seconds) -------------------------------------
    _SURPRISE_WIN = 60      # 10 min of trailing volume history for the z-score
    _BETA_WIN = 120         # 20 min trailing loading on market-wide activity
    _RET_VOL_WIN = 60       # trailing return-vol normaliser
    _PATH_WIN = 12          # 2 min recent path over which impact is measured

    def calc(self, data: dict[str, pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame:
        close = data["close"]
        volume = data["volume"]

        # ---- 1. standardized volume surprise -----------------------------
        s = _volume_surprise(volume, self._SURPRISE_WIN)

        # ---- 2. market-wide ('negotiable pool') activity surprise --------
        med = s.median(axis=1)
        mdf = _broadcast_row(med.fillna(0.0), s)

        # ---- 3. causal decomposition into common vs specialist flow ------
        beta = _rolling_loading(s, mdf, self._BETA_WIN).fillna(1.0)
        f_common = (beta * mdf).replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan).fillna(0.0)
        f_idio = (s.fillna(0.0) - f_common).replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan).fillna(0.0)

        # ---- 4. return manufactured on each flow channel -----------------
        r = _vol_scaled_logret(close, self._RET_VOL_WIN)
        r_common = _flow_path_integral(f_common, r, self._PATH_WIN)
        r_idio = _flow_path_integral(f_idio, r, self._PATH_WIN)

        # robust cross-sectional standardisation of the two channels
        z_common = rank(r_common.replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)) - 0.5
        z_idio = rank(r_idio.replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)) - 0.5

        # ---- 5. eligibility gate -----------------------------------------
        elig = _eligibility(data, close)
        w_common = 0.5 + elig          # eligible names: deep anonymous pool -> rent reverses
        w_idio = 1.5 - elig            # rationed names: residual flow is the informed leg

        raw = (-w_common * z_common.fillna(0.0)) + (w_idio * z_idio.fillna(0.0))

        # ---- 6. sector neutralisation + validity mask --------------------
        sec = data.get("sector")
        if isinstance(sec, pd.DataFrame):
            groups = sec.reindex_like(close).astype(object).where(sec.notna(), "UNKNOWN")
            try:
                raw = indneutralize(raw, groups)
            except Exception:
                raw = raw.sub(raw.mean(axis=1), axis=0)
        else:
            raw = raw.sub(raw.mean(axis=1), axis=0)

        valid = s.notna() & r.notna() & close.notna()
        out = raw.replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan).where(valid)
        out = out.sub(out.mean(axis=1), axis=0)
        return out.astype(float)

    """Variance-ratio regime factor: fade names whose returns mean-revert."""

    from __future__ import annotations

    import numpy as np
    import pandas as pd

    from quant_fund_agent.factors.base import BaseFactor
    from quant_fund_agent.factors.ops import rank, returns
    from quant_fund_agent.factors.registry import register_factor


    def _variance_ratio(ret: pd.DataFrame, k: int, n: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Lo–MacKinlay variance ratio over horizon k, estimated on a trailing
        n-bar window.  VR < 1 => mean-reverting, VR > 1 => trending.  Causal:
        every term is a trailing rolling statistic, so value at t sees only <= t."""
        var_1 = ret.rolling(n, min_periods=n).var()
        k_ret = ret.rolling(k, min_periods=k).sum()          # overlapping k-bar returns
        var_k = k_ret.rolling(n, min_periods=n).var()
        return var_k / (k * var_1).replace(0.0, np.nan)


    @register_factor
    class VarianceRatioReversion(BaseFactor):
        factor_id = "variance_ratio_reversion"
        name = "Variance-ratio reversion"
        category = "mean_reversion"
        description = (
            "Cross-sectional rank of (1 - trailing variance ratio): long the "
            "most mean-reverting names, short the most trending ones."
        )
        window_length = 120
        inputs = ["close"]
        prediction_horizon = 12
        suggested_horizons = [6, 12, 24]

        def calc(self, data: dict[str, pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame:
            ret = returns(data)
            vr = _variance_ratio(ret, 5, 100)
            return rank(1.0 - vr)

def _xs_zscore(df: pd.DataFrame, clip: float = 5.0) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Cross-sectional (per-bar) z-score, robustly clipped."""
    mu = df.mean(axis=1)
    sd = df.std(axis=1).replace(0.0, np.nan)
    z = df.sub(mu, axis=0).div(sd, axis=0)
    return z.clip(-clip, clip)


def _group_codes(labels) -> np.ndarray:
    """Map a 1-d array of text labels to integer codes (-1 = missing)."""
    n = len(labels)
    codes = np.full(n, -1, dtype=np.int64)
    mapping: dict = {}
    for i in range(n):
        v = labels[i]
        if v is None:
            continue
        if isinstance(v, float) and not np.isfinite(v):
            continue
        s = str(v).strip()
        if s == "" or s.lower() == "nan" or s.lower() == "none":
            continue
        code = mapping.get(s)
        if code is None:
            code = len(mapping)
            mapping[s] = code
        codes[i] = code
    return codes


def _corr_matrix(win: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Pearson correlation matrix of the columns of a trailing return window."""
    X = np.where(np.isfinite(win), win, 0.0).astype(float)
    X = X - X.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)
    sd = X.std(axis=0)
    sd = np.where(sd > 0.0, sd, np.nan)
    Xn = X / sd
    Xn = np.where(np.isfinite(Xn), Xn, 0.0)
    C = (Xn.T @ Xn) / float(max(X.shape[0], 1))
    C = np.where(np.isfinite(C), C, 0.0)
    return np.clip(C, -1.0, 1.0)

        same = (codes[:, None] == codes[None, :]) & valid[:, None] & valid[None, :]
        A[same] = 1.0
    if n > 1 and topk > 0:
        C = corr.copy()
        np.fill_diagonal(C, -np.inf)
        k = int(min(topk, n - 1))
        idx = np.argpartition(-C, k - 1, axis=1)[:, :k]
        rows = np.repeat(np.arange(n), k)
        A[rows, idx.ravel()] = 1.0
    A = np.maximum(A, A.T)
    np.fill_diagonal(A, 0.0)
    return A


def _darcy_laplacian(A: np.ndarray, K: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Weighted graph Laplacian with edge conductance = harmonic mean of K.

    This is the discrete analogue of -div(K grad .) on the peer network: an edge
    between two illiquid (low-K) nodes barely transmits flow, so pressure piles
    up there exactly as in the heterogeneous Darcy problem.
    """
    Kp = np.where(np.isfinite(K) & (K > 0.0), K, np.nan)
    med = np.nanmedian(Kp) if np.isfinite(Kp).any() else np.nan
    if not np.isfinite(med) or med <= 0.0:
        med = 1.0
    Kn = Kp / med
    Kn = np.where(np.isfinite(Kn), Kn, 1.0)
    Kn = np.clip(Kn, 1e-4, 1e4)
    num = 2.0 * np.outer(Kn, Kn)
    den = Kn[:, None] + Kn[None, :]
    H = num / np.where(den > 0.0, den, np.nan)
    H = np.where(np.isfinite(H), H, 0.0)
    C = A * H
    C = 0.5 * (C + C.T)
    np.fill_diagonal(C, 0.0)
    return np.diag(C.sum(axis=1)) - C


def _solve_zero_mean(L: np.ndarray, F: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Solve L p = f under a zero-mean constraint for a block of sources.

    ``F`` is (n_names, n_bars).  L is singular (constant null space), so we damp
    it by a tiny ridge and project the solution back to zero mean, which is the
    pseudo-inverse solution for zero-mean right-hand sides.
    """
    n = L.shape[0]
    diag_scale = float(np.mean(np.diag(L)))
    if not np.isfinite(diag_scale) or diag_scale <= 0.0:
        diag_scale = 1.0
    eps = 1e-6 * diag_scale + 1e-12
    M = L + eps * np.eye(n)
    Fz = F - F.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)
    try:
        P = linalg.solve(M, Fz, assume_a="pos")
    except Exception:
        try:
            P = np.linalg.lstsq(M, Fz, rcond=None)[0]
        except Exception:
            return np.full_like(Fz, np.nan)
    P = np.where(np.isfinite(P), P, 0.0)
    return P - P.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)

    def _variance_ratio(ret: pd.DataFrame, k: int, n: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Lo–MacKinlay variance ratio over horizon k, estimated on a trailing
        n-bar window.  VR < 1 => mean-reverting, VR > 1 => trending.  Causal:
        every term is a trailing rolling statistic, so value at t sees only <= t."""
        var_1 = ret.rolling(n, min_periods=n).var()
        k_ret = ret.rolling(k, min_periods=k).sum()          # overlapping k-bar returns
        var_k = k_ret.rolling(n, min_periods=n).var()
        return var_k / (k * var_1).replace(0.0, np.nan)


    @register_factor
    class VarianceRatioReversion(BaseFactor):
        factor_id = "variance_ratio_reversion"
        name = "Variance-ratio reversion"
        category = "mean_reversion"
        description = (

        inputs = ["close"]
        prediction_horizon = 12
        suggested_horizons = [6, 12, 24]

        def calc(self, data: dict[str, pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame:

            vr = _variance_ratio(ret, 5, 100)
            return rank(1.0 - vr)

from __future__ import annotations

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from quant_fund_agent.factors.base import BaseFactor
from quant_fund_agent.factors.ops import delay, rank, ts_sum
from quant_fund_agent.factors.registry import register_factor


def _clean(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Replace non-finite entries by NaN (defensive plumbing only)."""
    return df.replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)


def _xs_pref_attachment_fit(
    y: pd.DataFrame, x: pd.DataFrame, min_names: int = 8
) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.Series]:
    """Per-bar cross-sectional fit of the mixed preferential-attachment map.

    Model for name i at bar t (shares sum to one across names):

        share_t(i) = gamma_t * (1 / N_t)  +  (1 - gamma_t) * share_{t-W}(i)

    which is exactly an affine cross-sectional regression of the current volume
    share on the *lagged, disjoint-window* share: intercept a_t = gamma_t / N_t and
    slope b_t = 1 - gamma_t (the exploitation intensity).  Solving it row-by-row with
    closed-form OLS gives

        residual_t(i) = actual share - proportional (exploitation) prediction,

    i.e. the 'exploration' / discovery component of the name's attention, and the
    slope b_t = 1 - gamma_t which is the market-wide exploitation intensity
    (implied tail exponent alpha_t = 1 + 1 / b_t, close to 2 when b_t -> 1).

    Purely cross-sectional per row, so no time information leaks: value at t uses
    only quantities built from trailing windows ending at t.
    """
    y = _clean(y)
    x = _clean(x)
    valid = y.notna() & x.notna()

    yv = y.where(valid)
    xv = x.where(valid)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)

    ybar = yv.mean(axis=1)
    xbar = xv.mean(axis=1)
    dy = yv.sub(ybar, axis=0)
    dx = xv.sub(xbar, axis=0)

    sxy = (dx * dy).sum(axis=1, min_count=1)
    sxx = (dx * dx).sum(axis=1, min_count=1)
    slope = sxy / sxx.replace(0.0, np.nan)
    slope = slope.where(n >= min_names)

    resid = dy.sub(dx.mul(slope, axis=0))
    resid = resid.where(valid)
    return resid, slope


def _row_z(df: pd.DataFrame, min_names: int = 8) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Cross-sectional (per-bar) standardisation; NaN rows with too few names."""
    df = _clean(df)
    n = df.notna().sum(axis=1)
    mu = df.mean(axis=1)
    sd = df.std(axis=1).replace(0.0, np.nan)
    z = df.sub(mu, axis=0).div(sd, axis=0)
    return z.where(n >= min_names)


@register_factor
class PreferentialAttachmentAttentionResidualSplit(BaseFactor):
    """Continue moves carried by excess-attention (exploration) volume, fade moves carried by merely proportional (exploitation) volume, gated by the cross-sectionally implied exploitation intensity 1 - gamma."""

    factor_id = "preferential_attachment_attention_residual_split"
    name = "Preferential-Attachment Attention Residual with Exploration-Rate Gate"
    category = "microstructure"
    description = (
        "Over a rolling window, computes each name's share of total market volume and "
        "the share predicted by a one-parameter mixed preferential-attachment fit "
        "(uniform-exploration weight gamma_t estimated cross-sectionally each bar from "
        "current share on lagged share); the standardized attention residual (actual "
        "minus predicted share) is then interacted with the name's cross-sectionally "
        "demeaned window return and scaled by the implied exploitation intensity "
        "(1 - gamma_t, equivalently proximity of the implied tail exponent to 2), "
        "giving continuation for excess-attention movers and reversal for "
        "proportional-flow movers."
    )
    window_length = 90
    inputs = ["close", "volume"]
    prediction_horizon = 6
    suggested_horizons = [6]

    # attention-accumulation window (bars); two disjoint windows are used
    _W = 30
    _MIN_NAMES = 8

    def calc(self, data: dict[str, pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame:
        close = _clean(data["close"].astype(float))
        volume = _clean(data["volume"].astype(float)).fillna(0.0).clip(lower=0.0)

        W = int(self._W)
        px = close.where(close > 0.0)
        tradable = px.notna()

        # ---- attention shares -------------------------------------------------
        # trailing W-bar volume, normalised into a market share (sums to 1 per bar)
        vol_w = ts_sum(volume, W)
        vol_w = vol_w.where(tradable)
        total = vol_w.sum(axis=1, min_count=1).replace(0.0, np.nan)
        share = vol_w.div(total, axis=0)

        # popularity measured on the *previous, disjoint* window -> strictly causal
        share_lag = delay(share, W)

        # ---- mixed preferential-attachment fit (per bar, cross-sectional) -----
        resid, slope = _xs_pref_attachment_fit(share, share_lag, self._MIN_NAMES)

        # exploitation intensity b_t = 1 - gamma_t in [0, 1]; smoothed in time only
        # with a trailing EWM (no look-ahead) to tame per-bar estimation noise.
        expl = slope.clip(lower=0.0, upper=1.0)
        expl = expl.ewm(halflife=12.0, min_periods=1).mean().fillna(0.0)

        # standardized exploration (excess-attention) residual
        z_res = _row_z(resid, self._MIN_NAMES).clip(-4.0, 4.0)

        # ---- the move that the attention accompanied -------------------------
        log_px = np.log(px)
        ret_w = log_px - log_px.shift(W)
        z_ret = _row_z(ret_w, self._MIN_NAMES).clip(-4.0, 4.0)

        # ---- split: continuation on exploration flow, reversal on proportional flow
        raw = (z_res * z_ret).where(tradable)

        tilt = rank(raw) - 0.5
        signal = tilt.mul(expl, axis=0)

        signal = _clean(signal).where(tradable)
        signal = signal.reindex(index=close.index, columns=close.columns)
        return signal.fillna(0.0)

    def _variance_ratio(ret: pd.DataFrame, k: int, n: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Lo–MacKinlay variance ratio over horizon k, estimated on a trailing
        n-bar window.  VR < 1 => mean-reverting, VR > 1 => trending.  Causal:

        return var_k / (k * var_1).replace(0.0, np.nan)

is computed twice: once at native (1-bar) resolution and once on the k-bar
block increments that a coarse sampler would see.  Their difference Γ =

from __future__ import annotations

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from quant_fund_agent.factors.base import BaseFactor
from quant_fund_agent.factors.ops import rank, stddev, ts_mean, ts_sum
from quant_fund_agent.factors.registry import register_factor


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# tunables (10-second bars; horizon = 6 bars = 1 minute)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
_W = 60      # rolling path window (10 minutes of 10s bars)
_K = 6       # coarse block size (1 minute)  ->  _W / _K = 10 blocks
_NORM = 120  # trailing window used to put both channels on a common scale
_CAP = 6.0   # winsorisation cap on normalised increments


def _orientation(open_: pd.DataFrame,
                 high: pd.DataFrame,
                 low: pd.DataFrame,
                 close: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Bar orientation in [-1, 1]: sign of the body plus an OHLC shape term.

    ``(close + open - high - low) / (high - low)`` is the classic sub-bar path
    orientation proxy: +1 when the bar opened and closed near its high (buying
    pressure sustained inside the bar), -1 when it lived near its low.  It is a
    within-bar statistic, hence strictly causal at the bar close.
    """
    rng = (high - low)
    rng = rng.where(rng > 0.0)
    shape = ((close + open_ - high - low) / rng).clip(-1.0, 1.0)
    body = np.sign(close - open_)
    return 0.5 * (body.fillna(0.0) + shape.fillna(0.0))


def _normalise(inc: pd.DataFrame, n: int, cap: float) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Scale increments by their own trailing standard deviation and winsorise."""
    sd = stddev(inc, n).replace(0.0, np.nan)
    return (inc / sd).clip(-cap, cap), sd


def _shift_block_sum(df: pd.DataFrame, k: int, m: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Sum of ``df`` sampled every k bars: df_t + df_{t-k} + ... + df_{t-(m-1)k}."""
    out = df
    for j in range(1, m):
        out = out + df.shift(j * k)
    return out


def _levy_areas(dx: pd.DataFrame,
                dy: pd.DataFrame,
                w: int,
                k: int) -> tuple:
    """Trailing discrete Lévy area of the (x, y) path at fine and block resolution.

    For a window covering the increments of bars s+1..t (s = t-w):

        A = 0.5 * sum_u [ (x_{u-1} - x_s) dy_u - (y_{u-1} - y_s) dx_u ]

    which expands into a trailing rolling sum plus an origin correction that is
    identical for the fine and the coarse construction (so it cancels exactly in
    the defect Γ).  The coarse version replaces the per-bar increments by the
    k-bar block increments an endpoint-only sampler would observe.
    """
    m = int(w // k)

    x = dx.fillna(0.0).cumsum()
    y = dy.fillna(0.0).cumsum()

    x_prev = x.shift(1)
    y_prev = y.shift(1)
    d_x = x - x_prev
    d_y = y - y_prev

    # per-bar contribution to the fine area
    g = 0.5 * (x_prev * d_y - y_prev * d_x)
    fine_core = ts_sum(g, w)

    # per-block contribution (block ends at u, starts at u-k)
    x_k = x.shift(k)
    y_k = y.shift(k)
    h = 0.5 * (x_k * (y - y_k) - y_k * (x - x_k))
    coarse_core = _shift_block_sum(h, k, m)

    # origin correction (same for both resolutions)
    x_s = x.shift(w)
    y_s = y.shift(w)
    disp_x = x - x_s
    disp_y = y - y_s
    origin = 0.5 * (x_s * disp_y - y_s * disp_x)

    a_fine = fine_core - origin
    a_coarse = coarse_core - origin
    return a_fine, a_coarse, disp_x, disp_y


def _xs_orthogonalize(y: pd.DataFrame, x: pd.DataFrame, min_names: int = 10) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Row-wise (cross-sectional) residual of y on x — contemporaneous, causal."""
    valid = y.notna() & x.notna()
    yv = y.where(valid)
    xv = x.where(valid)
    yc = yv.sub(yv.mean(axis=1), axis=0)
    xc = xv.sub(xv.mean(axis=1), axis=0)
    cov = (yc * xc).mean(axis=1)
    var = (xc * xc).mean(axis=1).replace(0.0, np.nan)
    beta = (cov / var).fillna(0.0)
    cnt = valid.sum(axis=1)
    beta = beta.where(cnt >= min_names, 0.0)
    resid = yc - xc.mul(beta, axis=0)
    base = y.sub(y.mean(axis=1), axis=0)
    return resid.where(resid.notna(), base)


@register_factor
class WongZakaiAreaAnomalySubBlockRotationDrift(BaseFactor):
    """Sub-block Lévy-area defect between the price and order-flow channels."""

    factor_id = "wong_zakai_area_anomaly_subblock_rotation_drift"
    name = "Wong–Zakai Area Anomaly: Sub-Block Price/Flow Rotation Drift"
    category = "microstructure"
    description = (
        "Builds two causal channels per name over a rolling window — x = cumulative log "
        "return, y = cumulative volume-normalised signed flow (volume x sign(close-open), "
        "with a sub-bar OHLC shape correction from (close+open-high-low) capturing "
        "intra-bar path orientation) — computes the discrete Lévy area "
        "0.5*sum(x_{t-1}dy_t - y_{t-1}dx_t) at native bar resolution and again on k-bar "
        "block increments, and takes the anomaly Γ = A_fine - A_coarse; the "
        "cross-sectionally ranked Γ, sign-oriented by and gated on the magnitude of the "
        "coarse net displacement, is the signal."
    )
    window_length = 240
    inputs = ["open", "high", "low", "close", "volume"]
    prediction_horizon = 6
    suggested_horizons = [6]

    def calc(self, data: dict[str, pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame:
        close = data["close"]
        open_ = data["open"]
        high = data["high"]
        low = data["low"]
        volume = data["volume"]

        # ---- price channel increments -------------------------------------
        px = close.where(close > 0.0)
        log_px = np.log(px)
        dx_raw = log_px.diff()
        dx, sd_x = _normalise(dx_raw, _NORM, _CAP)

        # ---- order-flow channel increments --------------------------------
        orient = _orientation(open_, high, low, close)
        vol = volume.fillna(0.0).clip(lower=0.0)
        advol = ts_mean(vol, _NORM).replace(0.0, np.nan)
        dy_raw = (vol * orient) / advol
        dy, sd_y = _normalise(dy_raw, _NORM, _CAP)

        # ---- fine vs coarse (Wong–Zakai) Lévy areas -----------------------
        a_fine, a_coarse, disp_x, _disp_y = _levy_areas(dx, dy, _W, _K)
        gamma = a_fine - a_coarse          # the area defect destroyed by block sampling

        # ---- orientation by the coarse net displacement --------------------
        # gamma > 0  => price rotated ahead of flow inside the blocks
        #               (unsupported displacement -> snap-back),
        # gamma < 0  => flow rotated ahead of price (impact still to be paid -> drift).
        s_disp = np.sign(disp_x)
        score = -gamma * s_disp
        coarse_ctrl = -a_coarse * s_disp
        disp_mag = disp_x.abs()

        # ---- falsifiability guard: strip the coarse-area and displacement -
        # information cross-sectionally, so only the *defect* can trade.
        r_score = rank(score)
        r_coarse = rank(coarse_ctrl)
        r_disp = rank(disp_mag)
        resid = _xs_orthogonalize(r_score, r_coarse)
        resid = _xs_orthogonalize(resid, r_disp)

        # ---- soft gate on displacement magnitude ---------------------------
        gate = ((r_disp - 0.20) / 0.80).clip(0.0, 1.0).fillna(0.0)

        sig = (rank(resid) - 0.5) * gate

        # ---- validity mask & cross-sectional demeaning ---------------------
        valid = (
            close.notna()
            & sd_x.notna()
            & sd_y.notna()
            & advol.notna()
            & gamma.notna()
        )
        sig = sig.where(valid)
        sig = sig.sub(sig.mean(axis=1), axis=0)
        return sig.reindex(index=close.index, columns=close.columns)

    """Variance-ratio regime factor: fade names whose returns mean-revert."""

    from __future__ import annotations

    import numpy as np
    import pandas as pd

    from quant_fund_agent.factors.base import BaseFactor
    from quant_fund_agent.factors.ops import rank, returns
    from quant_fund_agent.factors.registry import register_factor


    def _variance_ratio(ret: pd.DataFrame, k: int, n: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Lo–MacKinlay variance ratio over horizon k, estimated on a trailing
        n-bar window.  VR < 1 => mean-reverting, VR > 1 => trending.  Causal:
        every term is a trailing rolling statistic, so value at t sees only <= t."""
        var_1 = ret.rolling(n, min_periods=n).var()
        k_ret = ret.rolling(k, min_periods=k).sum()          # overlapping k-bar returns
        var_k = k_ret.rolling(n, min_periods=n).var()
        return var_k / (k * var_1).replace(0.0, np.nan)


    @register_factor
    class VarianceRatioReversion(BaseFactor):
        factor_id = "variance_ratio_reversion"
        name = "Variance-ratio reversion"
        category = "mean_reversion"
        description = (
            "Cross-sectional rank of (1 - trailing variance ratio): long the "
            "most mean-reverting names, short the most trending ones."
        )
        window_length = 120
        inputs = ["close"]
        prediction_horizon = 12
        suggested_horizons = [6, 12, 24]

        def calc(self, data: dict[str, pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame:
            ret = returns(data)
            vr = _variance_ratio(ret, 5, 100)
            return rank(1.0 - vr)

def _dollar_neutral(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Cross-sectionally demean and rescale each row so sum(|w|) == 1.

    Purely per-row (no time information), so it cannot leak.
    """
    valid = df.notna()
    cnt = valid.sum(axis=1)
    centred = df.sub(df.mean(axis=1), axis=0)
    centred = centred.where(valid, 0.0)
    centred = centred.mul(cnt.gt(1).astype(float), axis=0)
    denom = centred.abs().sum(axis=1).replace(0.0, np.nan)
    out = centred.div(denom, axis=0)
    return out.replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan).fillna(0.0)


def _rolling_ridge_forecast(
    y: pd.Series,
    Z: pd.DataFrame,
    X: pd.DataFrame,
    n: int,
    mp: int,
    lam: float,
) -> pd.Series:
    """Trailing ridge-shrunk multivariate regression, evaluated out-of-sample.

    ``y[t]`` is the *already realized* h-bar premium ending at t and ``Z[t]`` are
    the AR predictors as they stood h bars earlier, so every (Z, y) pair used at
    time t is fully observable at t.  The fitted coefficients are then applied to
    the *current* predictor row ``X[t]`` to forecast the next h-bar premium.

    Estimation is closed-form on trailing centred cross-moments:
        b = (S + lam * tr(S)/K * I)^{-1} c
    with S the predictor covariance and c the predictor/target covariance, i.e.
    a ridge whose penalty is scale-free in the (tiny) 10-second return units.
    """
    T = len(y)
    K = Z.shape[1]
    if T == 0 or K == 0:
        return pd.Series(np.nan, index=y.index)

    my = y.rolling(n, min_periods=mp).mean()
    mz = Z.rolling(n, min_periods=mp).mean()

    S = np.full((T, K, K), np.nan, dtype=float)
    for i in range(K):
        zi = Z.iloc[:, i]
        for j in range(i, K):
            zj = Z.iloc[:, j]
            sij = (zi * zj).rolling(n, min_periods=mp).mean() - mz.iloc[:, i] * mz.iloc[:, j]
            vij = sij.to_numpy(dtype=float)
            S[:, i, j] = vij
            S[:, j, i] = vij

    c = np.full((T, K), np.nan, dtype=float)
    for i in range(K):
        ci = (Z.iloc[:, i] * y).rolling(n, min_periods=mp).mean() - mz.iloc[:, i] * my
        c[:, i] = ci.to_numpy(dtype=float)

    tr = np.trace(S, axis1=1, axis2=2) / float(K)
    with np.errstate(invalid="ignore"):
        good_tr = np.isfinite(tr) & (tr > 0.0)
    ridge = np.where(good_tr, lam * np.abs(tr), 0.0) + 1e-24

    eye = np.eye(K, dtype=float)[None, :, :]
    S_reg = S + ridge[:, None, None] * eye

    valid = (
        np.isfinite(S_reg).all(axis=(1, 2))
        & np.isfinite(c).all(axis=1)
        & good_tr
    )

    S_safe = np.where(valid[:, None, None], S_reg, np.broadcast_to(eye, S_reg.shape))
    c_safe = np.where(valid[:, None], c, 0.0)

    b = np.einsum("tij,tj->ti", np.linalg.pinv(S_safe), c_safe)
    b[~valid, :] = np.nan

    fc = my.to_numpy(dtype=float).copy()
    for i in range(K):
        xi = X.iloc[:, i].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        mzi = mz.iloc[:, i].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        fc = fc + b[:, i] * (xi - mzi)

    return pd.Series(fc, index=y.index)

        "debtGrowth/netStockIssuance, computes its bar-by-bar realized premium, "
        "forecasts the next-6-bar premium with a rolling ridge-shrunk AR "
        "regression scaled by inverse rolling premium variance (with negative "
        "forecasts shrunk and the multiplier EWMA-smoothed), and outputs each "
        "stock's exposure (blend of its characteristic weight and its causal "
        "rolling beta to the basket return) multiplied by that timing multiplier."

    def calc(self, data: dict[str, pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame:

        ret = close.pct_change()

        specs = [
            ("assetGrowth", False),
            ("capexToRevenue", True),   # capex is signed negative in the feed
            ("debtGrowth", False),
            ("netStockIssuance", False),
        ]
        rank_sum = pd.DataFrame(0.0, index=idx, columns=cols)
        rank_cnt = pd.DataFrame(0.0, index=idx, columns=cols)
        for field, use_abs in specs:
            raw = data.get(field)
            if raw is None:
                continue
            x = raw.reindex(index=idx, columns=cols)
            x = x.replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)
            if use_abs:
                x = x.abs()
            r = rank(x) - 0.5
            rank_sum = rank_sum.add(r.fillna(0.0), fill_value=0.0)
            rank_cnt = rank_cnt.add(r.notna().astype(float), fill_value=0.0)

        prem = prem.replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan).fillna(0.0)

        f2 = prem.rolling(3 * _H, min_periods=3 * _H).mean()

        # negative expected-premium forecasts.

    def _variance_ratio(ret: pd.DataFrame, k: int, n: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Lo–MacKinlay variance ratio over horizon k, estimated on a trailing
        n-bar window.  VR < 1 => mean-reverting, VR > 1 => trending.  Causal:
        every term is a trailing rolling statistic, so value at t sees only <= t."""
        var_1 = ret.rolling(n, min_periods=n).var()
        k_ret = ret.rolling(k, min_periods=k).sum()          # overlapping k-bar returns
        var_k = k_ret.rolling(n, min_periods=n).var()
        return var_k / (k * var_1).replace(0.0, np.nan)

    class VarianceRatioReversion(BaseFactor):

from __future__ import annotations

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from quant_fund_agent.factors.base import BaseFactor
from quant_fund_agent.factors.ops import adv, rank, stddev, ts_mean, ts_sum
from quant_fund_agent.factors.registry import register_factor


def _cs_standardize(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Cross-sectional demean / scale per bar (row-wise); clipped for robustness."""
    mu = df.mean(axis=1)
    sd = df.std(axis=1).replace(0.0, np.nan)
    z = df.sub(mu, axis=0).div(sd, axis=0)
    return z.clip(-4.0, 4.0)


def _pair_moments(
    x: np.ndarray, valid: np.ndarray, lag: int, chunk: int = 512
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Per-bar pooled cross-moments for the one-step map x_{t} ~ A x_{t-lag}.

    Returns (G, S, cnt) where at bar t:
        G[t] = sum_n x_{n,t-lag} x_{n,t-lag}'   (k x k)
        S[t] = sum_n x_{n,t}     x_{n,t-lag}'   (k x k)
        cnt[t] = number of pooled observations contributing at bar t
    Only information available at t is used (positive lags only).
    """
    T, _, k = x.shape
    G = np.zeros((T, k, k), dtype=np.float64)
    S = np.zeros((T, k, k), dtype=np.float64)
    cnt = np.zeros(T, dtype=np.float64)
    for s in range(0, T, chunk):
        e = min(T, s + chunk)
        s0 = max(s, lag)
        if s0 >= e:
            continue
        m = (valid[s0:e] & valid[s0 - lag : e - lag]).astype(np.float64)
        cur = x[s0:e].astype(np.float64) * m[:, :, None]
        lg = x[s0 - lag : e - lag].astype(np.float64) * m[:, :, None]
        G[s0:e] = np.einsum("tnk,tnj->tkj", lg, lg, optimize=True)
        S[s0:e] = np.einsum("tnk,tnj->tkj", cur, lg, optimize=True)
        cnt[s0:e] = m.sum(axis=1)
    return G, S, cnt


def _direct_moments(
    x: np.ndarray,
    valid: np.ndarray,
    y: np.ndarray,
    yvalid: np.ndarray,
    h: int,
    chunk: int = 512,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Per-bar pooled cross-moments for the direct h-step map y_{s} ~ w' x_{s}.

    y[t] is the *realized* h-bar cumulative (standardized) return ending at t, so it
    is the target of the state observed h bars earlier.  The contribution booked at
    bar t therefore pairs x_{t-h} with y_t -- both known at t.
    """
    T, _, k = x.shape
    G = np.zeros((T, k, k), dtype=np.float64)
    B = np.zeros((T, k), dtype=np.float64)
    cnt = np.zeros(T, dtype=np.float64)
    for s in range(0, T, chunk):
        e = min(T, s + chunk)
        s0 = max(s, h)
        if s0 >= e:
            continue
        m = (valid[s0 - h : e - h] & yvalid[s0:e]).astype(np.float64)
        xs = x[s0 - h : e - h].astype(np.float64) * m[:, :, None]
        ys = y[s0:e] * m
        G[s0:e] = np.einsum("tnk,tnj->tkj", xs, xs, optimize=True)
        B[s0:e] = np.einsum("tnk,tn->tk", xs, ys, optimize=True)
        cnt[s0:e] = m.sum(axis=1)
    return G, B, cnt


def _roll_sum(a: np.ndarray, w: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Trailing rolling sum along axis 0 (expanding until the window fills)."""
    cs = np.cumsum(a, axis=0)
    out = cs.copy()
    if a.shape[0] > w:
        out[w:] = cs[w:] - cs[:-w]
    return out


def _batched_ridge_inverse(g: np.ndarray, lam: float) -> np.ndarray:
    """Pseudo-inverse of (G + lam * mean-diag * I) for a small batch of Gram matrices."""
    k = g.shape[-1]
    g = np.nan_to_num(g, nan=0.0, posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0)
    tr = np.trace(g, axis1=1, axis2=2) / float(k)
    tr = np.where(np.isfinite(tr) & (tr > 0.0), tr, 1.0)
    gr = g + (lam * tr)[:, None, None] * np.eye(k)[None, :, :]
    out = np.zeros_like(gr)
    for i in range(gr.shape[0]):
        try:
            out[i] = np.linalg.pinv(gr[i])
        except np.linalg.LinAlgError:
            out[i] = np.zeros((k, k), dtype=np.float64)
    return out


def _spectral_radius(a: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Max |eigenvalue| of each matrix in a small batch (non-finite -> +inf)."""
    n = a.shape[0]
    rho = np.full(n, np.inf, dtype=np.float64)
    for i in range(n):
        m = a[i]
        if not np.all(np.isfinite(m)):
            continue
        try:
            ev = np.linalg.eigvals(m)
        except np.linalg.LinAlgError:
            continue
        if np.all(np.isfinite(ev)):
            rho[i] = float(np.max(np.abs(ev)))
    return rho


def _apply_coef(x: np.ndarray, coef: np.ndarray, chunk: int = 512) -> np.ndarray:
    """Per-bar linear map: out[t, n] = sum_k coef[t, k] * x[t, n, k]."""
    T, N, _ = x.shape
    out = np.zeros((T, N), dtype=np.float64)
    for s in range(0, T, chunk):
        e = min(T, s + chunk)
        out[s:e] = np.einsum(
            "tnk,tk->tn", x[s:e].astype(np.float64), coef[s:e], optimize=True
        )
    return out


@register_factor
class DirectVsRecursiveMultistepForecastWedge(BaseFactor):
    """Wedge between a direct 6-bar forecast and the recursively-iterated one-step forecast."""

    factor_id = "direct_vs_recursive_multistep_forecast_wedge"
    name = "Direct-minus-Recursive Multi-Horizon Forecast Wedge"
    category = "statistical_arbitrage"
    description = (
        "Per bar, build a small causal state vector per ticker (1-bar return, 3-bar "
        "return, volume-weighted signed return, range/realized-vol ratio, volume "
        "surprise), cross-sectionally demeaned and scaled; on a rolling causal window "
        "fit (a) a pooled one-step VAR companion map and iterate it 6 steps, and (b) a "
        "pooled direct ridge regression of the fully-realized 6-bar forward return on "
        "the same state (targets attached h bars later, so no look-ahead). The factor is "
        "the cross-sectional rank of (direct forecast - iterated recursive forecast), "
        "damped to zero when the companion matrix is non-stationary or the fit degenerate."
    )
    window_length = 600
    inputs = ["close", "high", "low", "volume"]
    prediction_horizon = 6
    suggested_horizons = [6]

    # estimation hyper-parameters (fixed, not learned)
    fit_window = 480      # bars of pooled moments in each trailing fit window
    refit_step = 30       # refit the maps every 30 bars, carry coefficients forward
    ridge_lambda = 5e-2   # ridge strength, relative to mean Gram diagonal
    min_pooled_obs = 200  # pooled (bar x ticker) observations required per fit

    def calc(self, data: dict[str, pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame:
        close = data["close"]
        index, columns = close.index, close.columns
        T, N = close.shape
        h = int(self.prediction_horizon)

        if T < (h + 30) or N < 3:
            return pd.DataFrame(np.nan, index=index, columns=columns)

        c = close.astype(float).replace(0.0, np.nan)
        high = data["high"].astype(float)
        low = data["low"].astype(float)
        vol = data["volume"].astype(float).clip(lower=0.0)

        # ---- causal state features -------------------------------------------
        lc = np.log(c)
        r1 = lc.diff(1)
        r3 = ts_sum(r1, 3)

        advol = adv(vol, 60).replace(0.0, np.nan)
        vratio = (vol / advol).clip(0.0, 50.0)
        lvr = np.log1p(vratio)

        sgn_flow = r1 * lvr                                  # volume-weighted signed return
        rvol = stddev(r1, 20).replace(0.0, np.nan)
        range_ratio = ((high - low).abs() / c) / rvol         # range / realized-vol
        vol_surprise = lvr - ts_mean(lvr, 60)                 # volume surprise

        feats = [
            _cs_standardize(r1),
            _cs_standardize(r3),
            _cs_standardize(sgn_flow),
            _cs_standardize(range_ratio),
            _cs_standardize(vol_surprise),
        ]
        k = len(feats)

        raw = [f.to_numpy(dtype=np.float64) for f in feats]
        valid = np.ones((T, N), dtype=bool)
        for a in raw:
            valid &= np.isfinite(a)

        X = np.zeros((T, N, k), dtype=np.float32)
        for i, a in enumerate(raw):
            filled = np.nan_to_num(a, nan=0.0, posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0)
            X[:, :, i] = np.where(valid, filled, 0.0).astype(np.float32)

        # realized h-bar cumulative standardized return ending at t (known at t)
        y_df = ts_sum(feats[0], h)
        y = y_df.to_numpy(dtype=np.float64)
        yvalid = np.isfinite(y)
        y = np.where(yvalid, y, 0.0)

        # ---- per-bar pooled moments, then trailing-window sums ---------------
        g_var, s_var, n_var = _pair_moments(X, valid, 1)
        g_dir, b_dir, n_dir = _direct_moments(X, valid, y, yvalid, h)

        w_win = int(self.fit_window)
        G_var = _roll_sum(g_var, w_win)
        S_var = _roll_sum(s_var, w_win)
        C_var = _roll_sum(n_var, w_win)
        G_dir = _roll_sum(g_dir, w_win)
        B_dir = _roll_sum(b_dir, w_win)
        C_dir = _roll_sum(n_dir, w_win)

        # ---- refit on a coarse causal grid, carry coefficients forward -------
        step = max(1, int(self.refit_step))
        grid = np.arange(0, T, step)

        gi_var = _batched_ridge_inverse(G_var[grid], float(self.ridge_lambda))
        gi_dir = _batched_ridge_inverse(G_dir[grid], float(self.ridge_lambda))

        S_g = np.nan_to_num(S_var[grid], nan=0.0, posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0)
        B_g = np.nan_to_num(B_dir[grid], nan=0.0, posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0)

        A = S_g @ gi_var                                  # one-step companion map
        A = np.nan_to_num(A, nan=0.0, posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0)
        A = np.clip(A, -10.0, 10.0)

        # iterate the one-step map: sum_{j=1..h} A^j  (the "recursive strategy")
        m_sum = A.copy()
        p = A.copy()
        for _ in range(h - 1):
            p = p @ A
            m_sum = m_sum + p
        rec_coef = m_sum[:, 0, :]                         # loading on the return component
        rec_coef = np.clip(np.nan_to_num(rec_coef, nan=0.0, posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0), -50.0, 50.0)

        dir_coef = (gi_dir @ B_g[:, :, None])[:, :, 0]     # direct h-step ridge map
        dir_coef = np.clip(np.nan_to_num(dir_coef, nan=0.0, posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0), -50.0, 50.0)

        # ---- damping: non-stationary iteration or degenerate window ----------
        rho = _spectral_radius(A)
        damp = np.clip((1.0 - rho) / 0.05, 0.0, 1.0)
        damp = np.where(np.isfinite(damp), damp, 0.0)
        min_obs = float(self.min_pooled_obs)
        ok = (
            (C_var[grid] >= min_obs)
            & (C_dir[grid] >= min_obs)
            & np.isfinite(rec_coef).all(axis=1)
            & np.isfinite(dir_coef).all(axis=1)
        )
        damp = np.where(ok, damp, 0.0)

        # map grid coefficients to every bar (grid point used is always <= t)
        pos = np.arange(T) // step
        dir_full = dir_coef[pos]
        rec_full = rec_coef[pos]
        damp_full = damp[pos]

        # ---- forecasts and the wedge ----------------------------------------
        f_direct = _apply_coef(X, dir_full)
        f_recursive = _apply_coef(X, rec_full)
        wedge = (f_direct - f_recursive) * damp_full[:, None]

        good = valid & (damp_full[:, None] > 0.0) & np.isfinite(wedge)
        wedge = np.where(good, wedge, np.nan)

        out = pd.DataFrame(wedge, index=index, columns=columns)
        return rank(out)
"}

    """Variance-ratio regime factor: fade names whose returns mean-revert."""

    from __future__ import annotations

    import numpy as np
    import pandas as pd

    from quant_fund_agent.factors.base import BaseFactor
    from quant_fund_agent.factors.ops import rank, returns
    from quant_fund_agent.factors.registry import register_factor


    def _variance_ratio(ret: pd.DataFrame, k: int, n: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Lo–MacKinlay variance ratio over horizon k, estimated on a trailing
        n-bar window.  VR < 1 => mean-reverting, VR > 1 => trending.  Causal:
        every term is a trailing rolling statistic, so value at t sees only <= t."""
        var_1 = ret.rolling(n, min_periods=n).var()
        k_ret = ret.rolling(k, min_periods=k).sum()          # overlapping k-bar returns
        var_k = k_ret.rolling(n, min_periods=n).var()
        return var_k / (k * var_1).replace(0.0, np.nan)


    @register_factor
    class VarianceRatioReversion(BaseFactor):
        factor_id = "variance_ratio_reversion"
        name = "Variance-ratio reversion"
        category = "mean_reversion"
        description = (
            "Cross-sectional rank of (1 - trailing variance ratio): long the "
            "most mean-reverting names, short the most trending ones."
        )
        window_length = 120
        inputs = ["close"]
        prediction_horizon = 12
        suggested_horizons = [6, 12, 24]

        def calc(self, data: dict[str, pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame:
            ret = returns(data)
            vr = _variance_ratio(ret, 5, 100)
            return rank(1.0 - vr)

def _cs_z(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Row-wise (cross-sectional) z-score, NaN-safe."""
    mu = df.mean(axis=1)
    sd = df.std(axis=1).replace(0.0, np.nan)
    return df.sub(mu, axis=0).div(sd, axis=0)


def _inv3_ridge(M: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Batched analytic inverse of (N,3,3) symmetric matrices with a ridge.

    A small trace-proportional ridge keeps the covariance well conditioned in
    the warm-up phase and for degenerate (constant-feature) tickers.
    """
    diag = np.diagonal(M, axis1=1, axis2=2)
    scale = np.maximum(np.nanmean(diag, axis=1), 1e-12)
    ridge = (1e-3 * scale + 1e-8)
    A = M + np.eye(3)[None, :, :] * ridge[:, None, None]

    a = A[:, 0, 0]
    b = A[:, 0, 1]
    c = A[:, 0, 2]
    d = A[:, 1, 0]
    e = A[:, 1, 1]
    f = A[:, 1, 2]
    g = A[:, 2, 0]
    h = A[:, 2, 1]
    i = A[:, 2, 2]

    c00 = e * i - f * h
    c10 = -(d * i - f * g)
    c20 = d * h - e * g
    det = a * c00 + b * c10 + c * c20
    det = np.where(np.abs(det) > 1e-18, det, np.nan)

    inv = np.empty_like(A)
    inv[:, 0, 0] = c00
    inv[:, 1, 0] = c10
    inv[:, 2, 0] = c20
    inv[:, 0, 1] = -(b * i - c * h)
    inv[:, 1, 1] = a * i - c * g
    inv[:, 2, 1] = -(a * h - b * g)
    inv[:, 0, 2] = b * f - c * e
    inv[:, 1, 2] = -(a * f - c * d)
    inv[:, 2, 2] = a * e - b * d
    return inv / det[:, None, None]


def _rls_step(P: np.ndarray, w: np.ndarray, x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray,
              lam: float, mask: np.ndarray):
    """One exponentially-weighted RLS update, vectorised across tickers.

    P: (N,K,K) inverse-correlation state, w: (N,K) coefficients,
    x: (N,K) regressors observed at t-1, y: (N,) target realised at t.
    Only rows where ``mask`` is True are advanced; others keep their state.
    """
    Px = np.einsum("nij,nj->ni", P, x)
    denom = lam + np.einsum("ni,ni->n", x, Px)
    denom = np.where(denom > 1e-12, denom, 1e-12)
    Pn = (P - Px[:, :, None] * Px[:, None, :] / denom[:, None, None]) / lam
    Pn = 0.5 * (Pn + np.transpose(Pn, (0, 2, 1)))
    Pn = np.clip(Pn, -1.0e6, 1.0e6)

    err = y - np.einsum("ni,ni->n", x, w)
    grad = np.einsum("nij,nj->ni", Pn, x) * err[:, None]
    wn = np.clip(w + grad, -1.0e4, 1.0e4)

    ok = mask & np.isfinite(err) & np.isfinite(wn).all(axis=1) & np.isfinite(Pn).all(axis=(1, 2))
    P_out = np.where(ok[:, None, None], Pn, P)
    w_out = np.where(ok[:, None], wn, w)
    err_out = np.where(ok, err, 0.0)
    return P_out, w_out, err_out, ok


def _dual_rls_wedge(X: np.ndarray, Y: np.ndarray, lam_fast: float, lam_slow: float,
                    kappa: float, a_short: float, a_long: float, burn: int):
    """Run the plastic / EWC-consolidated pair of RLS filters over the panel.

    X: (T,N,K) features known at each bar t.  Y: (T,N) realised (standardised)
    return of bar t.  The pair (X[t-1], Y[t]) is the only training example that
    is available at t, so the forecast stored at t uses X[t] and coefficients
    trained strictly on data up to t.  Returns (wedge, gate) arrays of (T,N).
    """
    T, N, K = X.shape
    wedge = np.full((T, N), np.nan)
    gate = np.full((T, N), np.nan)
    if T < 3 or N == 0:
        return wedge, gate

    finite_x = np.isfinite(X).all(axis=2)
    finite_y = np.isfinite(Y)
    Xf = np.where(np.isfinite(X), X, 0.0)
    Yf = np.where(finite_y, Y, 0.0)

    eye = np.eye(K)
    Pf = np.repeat((eye * 1.0e2)[None, :, :], N, axis=0)
    Ps = np.repeat((eye * 1.0e2)[None, :, :], N, axis=0)
    wf = np.zeros((N, K))
    ws = np.zeros((N, K))
    wbar = np.zeros((N, K))
    fisher = np.zeros((N, K))

    mu_s = np.zeros((N, K))
    mu_l = np.zeros((N, K))
    M_l = np.repeat(eye[None, :, :], N, axis=0)

    a_fish = 1.0 / 1500.0
    a_anch = 1.0 / 1500.0
    seen = np.zeros(N)

    with np.errstate(all="ignore"):
        for t in range(1, T):
            xprev = Xf[t - 1]
            ynow = Yf[t]
            m = finite_x[t - 1] & finite_y[t]

            # --- plastic (fast-forgetting) learner -------------------------
            Pf, wf, _, _ = _rls_step(Pf, wf, xprev, ynow, lam_fast, m)

            # --- slow learner + diagonal Fisher accumulation --------------
            Ps, ws, err_s, ok_s = _rls_step(Ps, ws, xprev, ynow, lam_slow, m)
            g2 = (xprev * err_s[:, None]) ** 2
            upd = ok_s[:, None]
            fisher = np.where(upd, (1.0 - a_fish) * fisher + a_fish * g2, fisher)
            wbar = np.where(upd, (1.0 - a_anch) * wbar + a_anch * ws, wbar)
            seen = seen + ok_s.astype(float)

            # --- EWC consolidation of the slow coefficients ---------------
            fmean = fisher.mean(axis=1)[:, None]
            fn = fisher / (fmean + 1e-18)
            pull = kappa * fn
            w_cons = (ws + pull * wbar) / (1.0 + pull)

            # --- replay / novelty gate (Mahalanobis, long-window metric) --
            xnow = Xf[t]
            Sigma = M_l - np.einsum("ni,nj->nij", mu_l, mu_l)
            Sinv = _inv3_ridge(Sigma)
            ds = xnow - mu_s
            dl = xnow - mu_l
            d2s = np.einsum("ni,nij,nj->n", ds, Sinv, ds)
            d2l = np.einsum("ni,nij,nj->n", dl, Sinv, dl)
            d2s = np.where(np.isfinite(d2s) & (d2s > 0.0), d2s, 0.0)
            d2l = np.where(np.isfinite(d2l) & (d2l > 0.0), d2l, 0.0)
            g_t = np.sqrt(d2s) / (1.0 + np.sqrt(d2l))

            live = finite_x[t] & (seen >= burn)
            f_plastic = np.einsum("ni,ni->n", xnow, wf)
            f_cons = np.einsum("ni,ni->n", xnow, w_cons)
            diff = f_cons - f_plastic
            wedge[t] = np.where(live & np.isfinite(diff), diff, np.nan)
            gate[t] = np.where(live, g_t, np.nan)

            # --- advance the replay statistics with the current state -----
            mx = finite_x[t][:, None]
            mu_s = np.where(mx, mu_s + a_short * (xnow - mu_s), mu_s)
            mu_l = np.where(mx, mu_l + a_long * (xnow - mu_l), mu_l)
            outer = np.einsum("ni,nj->nij", xnow, xnow)
            M_l = np.where(finite_x[t][:, None, None],
                           M_l + a_long * (outer - M_l), M_l)

    return wedge, gate


@register_factor
class EwcConsolidatedVsPlasticForecastWedge(BaseFactor):
    """Wedge between an EWC-consolidated and a fast-forgetting online forecast, gated by feature novelty."""

    factor_id = "ewc_consolidated_vs_plastic_forecast_wedge"
    name = "EWC-Consolidated vs Plastic Online-Forecast Wedge"
    category = "statistical_arbitrage"
    description = (
        "Per ticker, two recursive weighted least-squares predictors of next-bar "
        "return run causally on the same features (1-bar standardised return, "
        "signed volume pressure, intra-bar close location) with a fast forgetting "
        "factor (~30-bar memory, the plastic learner) and a slow one (~1500-bar "
        "memory); the slow coefficients are EWC-anchored toward their long-run "
        "means with per-coefficient weights proportional to accumulated squared "
        "gradients (diagonal Fisher importance). The factor is the "
        "cross-sectionally standardised consolidated-minus-plastic forecast "
        "difference, multiplied by a replay/novelty gate equal to the Mahalanobis "
        "distance of the current feature vector from its recent short-window "
        "centroid under the long-window covariance."
    )
    window_length = 1500
    inputs = ["open", "high", "low", "close", "volume"]
    prediction_horizon = 6
    suggested_horizons = [6]

    # memory of the two learners (forgetting factors) and EWC strength
    _mem_fast = 30.0
    _mem_slow = 1500.0
    _kappa = 2.0

    def calc(self, data: dict[str, pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame:
        close = data["close"]
        idx, cols = close.index, close.columns
        open_ = data["open"].reindex(index=idx, columns=cols)
        high = data["high"].reindex(index=idx, columns=cols)
        low = data["low"].reindex(index=idx, columns=cols)
        volume = data["volume"].reindex(index=idx, columns=cols)

        # ---- feature construction (all trailing / causal) ----------------
        ret = returns(data).reindex(index=idx, columns=cols)
        vol = stddev(ret, 300).replace(0.0, np.nan)
        f1 = (ret / vol).clip(-6.0, 6.0)

        advol = adv(volume, 300).replace(0.0, np.nan)
        f2 = (sign(close - open_) * volume / advol).clip(-6.0, 6.0)

        rng = (high - low).replace(0.0, np.nan)
        f3 = (2.0 * ((close - low) / rng - 0.5)).clip(-1.0, 1.0).fillna(0.0)

        X = np.stack(
            [
                f1.to_numpy(dtype=float),
                f2.to_numpy(dtype=float),
                f3.to_numpy(dtype=float),
            ],
            axis=2,
        )
        Y = f1.to_numpy(dtype=float)  # target: next bar's standardised return

        lam_fast = 1.0 - 1.0 / self._mem_fast
        lam_slow = 1.0 - 1.0 / self._mem_slow
        burn = 300

        wedge_arr, gate_arr = _dual_rls_wedge(
            X,
            Y,
            lam_fast,
            lam_slow,
            self._kappa,
            1.0 / 30.0,
            1.0 / 1500.0,
            burn,
        )

        wedge = pd.DataFrame(wedge_arr, index=idx, columns=cols)
        gate = pd.DataFrame(gate_arr, index=idx, columns=cols).clip(0.0, 5.0)

        z = _cs_z(wedge)
        signal = _cs_z(z * gate)
        return signal.replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan).fillna(0.0)

    def _variance_ratio(ret: pd.DataFrame, k: int, n: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Lo–MacKinlay variance ratio over horizon k, estimated on a trailing
        n-bar window.  VR < 1 => mean-reverting, VR > 1 => trending.  Causal:
